head: A 15-year-old in western Nepal paid for her village's new footbridge out of her own earnings.
summary: Sadiksha Oli spent Rs60,000 of her own money on a wooden footbridge over the Domai stream at Luma, in Bhume Rural Municipality of Rukum East, where the previous crossing was swept away in June. The money, earned through her monetised Facebook account, bought nails, corrugated iron sheets and the wages of skilled workers, while Oli, her relatives and neighbours cut local timber and finished the four-metre span in three days. The bridge restores the everyday walk between Luma and the ward office, the schools and the district headquarters, a route the stream cuts off whenever the monsoon fills it.

head: Farmers in a Texas panhandle town work a donated field for free and turn the harvest into tuition.
summary: Farmers and agricultural suppliers around Gruver, in the Texas panhandle, give their labour, machinery and inputs to plant and harvest a field the town's school owns, and the crops have paid out nearly $3 million in scholarships since 2016. The land came from Carl Nielsen, a Danish immigrant who bought it in the late 1800s and left it to Gruver school after his death in the 1970s; it was cash-leased for about $25,000 a year until a group of local farmers proposed in 2012 that they farm it themselves. Forty-eight of the students the fund has backed became the first in their families to finish college, and awards are pegged to West Texas A&M tuition of roughly $4,000 a semester and applied after other scholarships, so they also cover trade school and junior college.

head: A Nanaimo widow gave her husband's lifetime collection of instruments to a high school rock program.
summary: Sandy Rankin has given about $20,000 worth of drums, bass guitars and amplifiers, collected by her husband Harlow over a lifetime of playing, to the School of Rock program at John Barsby Community School in Nanaimo, British Columbia. Harlow Rankin died in April at 76 and had asked that the instruments go to students who could use them; his widow found them boxed up in the garage and went looking for a program that would take them. Russ Der, who has taught for 38 years and runs the program on a tight budget, has set up the extra kits in two upstairs rooms and will lend gear to students who cannot buy their own.

head: A Vermont couple gave away the 301 acres of woodland they spent a lifetime managing.
summary: Doug and Katharine Britton have given 301 acres of forest in Newbury, Vermont, to the Upper Valley Land Trust, which will hold the land permanently conserved and open to the public. The couple managed the hilly, entirely wooded parcel for timber for decades, planting about 30 acres of white pine in the 1950s among the red oak, balsam fir and sugar maple, and the transfer took 25 years to finalize. The gift joins roughly 1,300 acres of already protected land along a wildlife corridor where trust staff have found beaver and bear sign, and the trust plans to keep harvesting timber, extend two town trails across the property and support research on how animals move through it.

head: Phoebe Waller-Bridge bought a London flat and gave its use to playwrights starting out.
summary: Phoebe Waller-Bridge has bought a flat in London and donated its use to writers early in their careers, who will pay the bills and no rent. The flat is the centrepiece of Writers' Block, a pilot built by Sofie Mason and Diana Jervis-Read on the Adopt a Playwright Award they founded in 2008, which finds rooms for playwrights from low-income backgrounds who need to be in the capital for meetings, rehearsals and performances. Jack Thorne, James Graham, Sally Wainwright, Peter Morgan and Martin McDonagh are funding the pilot as well, and Graham, who slept on friends' floors and worked in call centres when he first came to London, said each spare room keeps a writer from giving up.

head: An Ottawa donor has given blood 500 times, 52 years after his first donation.
summary: Bob McDougall made his 500th donation to Canadian Blood Services on 2 November at the centre on Carling Avenue in Ottawa, 52 years after he first gave blood in 1974. He now gives plasma and platelets every two weeks, usually on a Monday, and Sandy Renny, a volunteer at the centre, said McDougall is the first person he sees each time he arrives for a shift. Canadian Blood Services, which says about 500 Canadians have reached the same mark, expects national demand for plasma to rise by half over the next five years, and McDougall said he will keep donating as long as his health allows.

head: A two-year public appeal has bought the 9,500-acre Rothbury Estate for nature.
summary: The Wildlife Trusts and Northumberland Wildlife Trust completed the £30m purchase of the entire 9,500-acre Rothbury Estate in Northumberland on 30 October, two years after opening their largest fundraising appeal. More than 25,000 people gave over £17m of that total, from across the UK and more than 50 countries including Finland, Barbados, Kenya and New Zealand, with the remainder coming from the National Lottery Heritage Fund, Defra and charitable trusts. The moorland, woods, river and working farms now stay in single ownership, and the trusts plan nature-friendly farming, habitat restoration and a greenway along a disused railway line, with volunteer soil and wildlife surveys starting this month.

head: A $30 million gift will expand the visitor center and education space at Kentucky's state botanical garden.
summary: The Bill Gatton Foundation has committed $30 million to the Arboretum, State Botanical Garden of Kentucky, the 100-acre public garden on the edge of the University of Kentucky's campus in Lexington. Foundation trustee Danny Dunn traced the gift to an earlier version of the will left by Bill Gatton, a university alumnus, and the money covers six projects, among them an expanded visitor center, an education building with two flex classrooms, a reconfigured entrance and improved walkways. The garden hosted at least 75 classes and more than 1,300 students last year, and its director, Michael Wall, expects construction to start in 2027 and run about a year.

head: An art historian gave Tate the 50 Indian paintings he spent his life assembling.
summary: The British art historian Charles Greig has donated 50 paintings and watercolours made in India during the 18th and 19th centuries to Tate, a collection he spent a working lifetime putting together. Alongside works by Ghulam Ali Khan, Johan Zoffany, Rudolf Swoboda and Thomas and William Daniell, the gift includes three watercolours by Sita Ram, who helped shape the European-style works known as Company paintings, and Greig said that at no stage did he see himself as other than a temporary steward. Tate Britain will open a free display drawn from the collection in 2028.

head: A Michigan family gave up 20 acres to make a 240-acre forest permanent.
summary: In Emmet County near Harbor Springs, Michigan, the Little Traverse Conservancy closed on 180 acres of hardwood forest after a $3 million community fundraising campaign, and the Ford family donated an additional 20 acres of its own land outright, permanently protecting 240 contiguous acres from development. The Fords have owned the property since the early 1980s and had let neighbors use it for walking and cross-country skiing for decades; conservancy development officer Emily Hughes said the deal takes any future sale to a developer off the table. The conservancy, which named the tract The Hundred Acre Wood, plans to build a parking area and expand the trail network next year, linking the preserve to an adjoining 80 acres already owned by West Traverse Township.
